newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: OPINION - Too early for Philippine inflation celebration.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Too early for Philippine inflation celebration.

text.p: University of the Philippines School of Economics

The Philippine government's fiscal and monetary authorities must be both perplexed and disappointed. Despite a series of feel-good economic news - higher GNP growth, lower unemployment and, more recently, a lower than expected inflation rate - the Manila stock market remained unimpressed. Under normal circumstances, such a mix of good news would have started a bull run. Yet foreign players have stopped buying while quite a number have unloaded and packed up.

As the September inflation rate was being unveiled, self-congratulatory statements were being issued by Philippine monetary and economic authorities from two distant places - Manila and Washington. It is not clear whether such self-congratulations are in order, however. Perhaps it's a bit too early for a celebration party.

Is the trend towards lower inflation sustainable? Let us look at the facts and their implications. A 4.4 percent inflation rate for September would move the actual average inflation closer to the government's revised target of 8.5 percent. But meeting this thrice-revised target will not be a cinch.

Despite the sharp drop in the inflation rate in September, the average inflation rate from January to September still stands at 9.7 percent. But that is still significantly higher than the government's original target of 5.0 percent (refer to the 1996 Budget Call and the revised Medium-Term Development Plan), or the adjusted inflation target of 6.0 to 7.0 percent (refer to the Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing). The bottom line is that the actual average inflation rate for 1996 will be higher than the 8.1 percent inflation rate in 1995 and the three sets of targets for 1996. That's retrogression, not progress.
What has to happen in order to meet the revised inflation target of 8.5 percent? Arithmetically, it means that inflation rates for October, November and December have to average 4.9 percent.

It would be tempting for government economists to claim that the 4.4 percent inflation rate for September may be sustained for the rest of the year. I disagree. The fact that it is the lowest in the series since June 1987 would suggest that it is far from the norm. To a large extent, the September inflation rate is the lowest because it is being compared to the consumer price index in September 1995 when the rice crisis was at its peak.

There are other reasons why the 4.4 percent inflation rate may not be sustainable. For one, it is almost certain that the expected drop in crude costs in the world market is not going to materialise. Energy officials earlier predicted that because of seasonality, crude costs and the price of oil products will soften by about this time of the year.

Short of a miracle, that will not happen because of Iraq's failure to reenter the world's oil supply and the unanticipated strong demand for oil products. As a result, oil products prices will go up this month and in the succeeding months.

The government may be tempted to postpone the increase in oil product prices - assuming the existing law would allow it. But that would be a mistake. It would mean a bigger budget deficit as the government would inevitably have to pay for the Oil Price Stabilisation Fund deficit. It would be inefficient as consumers will behave as if the Philippines is an oil producer rather than an oil importer and use oil products as if they were cheap. Worse, it would send a wrong signal to potential new players in the domestic oil industry that the government is not serious in its oil industry deregulation policy. Flip-flopping in this policy area is bound to be costly to the credibility of the government.

The downtrend in inflation is also not likely to continue owing to seasonality. Because of stong consumer demand during the Christmas season, the inflation rate would pick up towards year-end. The stronger purchasing power of consumers will be fuelled by the 13th month pay and Christmas bonuses to workers.

Finally, what does the inflation rate of 4.4 percent mean for the ordinary man in the street? First of all it does NOT mean that prices actually went down. What it means is that the increase in prices in September slowed down. But in Metro Manila, where about a fifth of Filipinos live, inflation rate remained high at 6.3 percent while in areas outside Metro Manila inflation rate has decelerated to 3.7 percent.
Here's my fearless forecast: Average annual inflation will be higher in 1996 than in 1995. By any measure, that kind of performance does not merit congratulations.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the view of Reuters)
